L32: # Fixed Point Homing Shuffles
L33: 
L34: Jonathan Parlett Drexel University, Philadelphia, USA
L35: ###### Abstract
L36: We study a family of maps from $S_{n}\to S_{n}$ we call fixed point homing shuffles. These maps generalize a few known problems such as Conway’s Topswops first described by Martin Gardner (1988), and a card shuffling process studied by Gweneth McKinley (2015). We show that the iterates of these homing shuffles always converge, and characterize the set $U_{n}$ of permutations that no homing shuffle sorts.
L37: We also study a homing shuffle that sorts anything not in $U_{n}$, and find how many iterations it takes to converge in the worst case.
L38: ###### Keywords:
L39: 
L40: Combinatorics, Permutations, Top-swops, Card Shuffling
L41: 
L42: ^{†}^{†}dmtcs-publicationdata: Volume vol. 27:1, Permutation Patterns 2024 (2025), #9, doi:10.46298/dmtcs.14653

L44: ## 1 Introduction
L45: ### 1.1 Card Games
L46: 
L47: Given a deck of playing cards labeled $1,2,\dots,n$, we may play a round of the topswops game as follows. If the top card of the deck is numbered $k$, we take the first $k$ cards from the top of the deck and then place them back on top in reverse order. We may repeat this process. For example, for a deck of $5$ cards arranged $43215$ (from top to bottom), we proceed as follows, underlining the cards that will be reversed on the next iteration.
L48:  | $\displaystyle\underline{342}15\to\underline{24}315\to\underline{4231}5\to\underline{1}3245.$  |
L49: We may note that any further rounds simply pick up the first card and put it back on the top. So the deck stays the same if the $1$-card is in front. The topswops game was proposed by John Conway [cite20†4 , Chapter Six]^{1}^{1} 1 The alternative spelling “topswaps” is also widespread., and subsequently addressed by Herbert Wilf, Donald Knuth, and recently by Linda Morales, and Hal Sudborough [cite20†4 , cite21†9 , cite22†11 ].
L50: In particular Wilf showed that, perhaps surprisingly, the $1$-card always eventually comes to the front in at most $2^{n-1}$ iterations [cite20†4 , Chapter Six, Appendix]. This bound was later improved by Knuth to the $f_{n+1}-1$ where $f_{n+1}$ is the $(n+1)$-th Fibonacci number [cite21†9 , §7.2.1.2, Exercise 108]. Recently a quadratic lower bound was shown by Morales and Sudborough [cite22†11 ].
L51: Topswops is also called the deterministic pancake problem [cite23†13 ], as it is related to the pancake problem where the goal is to sort a list using the minimal number of prefix reversals [cite24†1 , cite25†2 , cite26†5 , cite27†6 ].
L52: Topswops has some similarities with another card game studied by Gweneth McKinley in [cite28†10 ]. In this game, the front card $k$ is placed at position $k$ and every card lying in between simply moved one step upwards. For example, on our above deck, with the cards to be shifted underlined, the game proceeds as follows.
L53: 
L54:  | $$3\underline{42}15\to 4\underline{231}5\to 2\underline{3}145\to 3\underline{21}45\to 2\underline{1}345\to\underline{1}2345.$$  |
L55: The two games are similar in that they both involve moving the front card to its natural position in each step. The ultimate outcomes also have something in common: In both games, the $1$-card eventually lands in its natural position at the top of the deck, and the state remains the same after this point. McKinley showed that the $1$-card eventually comes to the front in at most $2^{n-1}-1$ iterations, and that this bound is tight.
L56: That is, there are decks such that it takes exactly $2^{n-1}-1$ turns for the $1$-card to come to the front. These similarities suggest a generalization we will explore in this work.
L57: ### 1.2 Contributions
L58: In this work we study a family of games that subsume the above. We show that, for any game in our family, the $1$-card always comes to the front in at most $2^{n-1}$ iterations, generalizing the results of Wilf and McKinley. We note that, for our above example, McKinley’s shuffle sorted the deck in question to its natural order $12345$, while Topswops did not. We characterize the decks that are not sortable by any game in our family, and exhibit a game that sorts all decks that are sortable.
L59: For this game, which we call max shuffle, we show that the $1$-card comes to the front in at most $2n-3$ iterations, and that this bound is tight. During the review process, we were informed that much of our results here are present in a prior work of Joyce Pechersky [cite29†12 ]. In particular, our Theorem cite30†4.7 and Theorem cite31†5.11 appear as Theorem 2 and Theorem 4 in [cite29†12 ]. Pechersky also studies our map $\mathcal{T}$ in more depth than we cover here. See Theorem 5 and Corollary 4 of [cite29†12 ].
L60: Our discussion of max shuffles remains a novel contribution, and we hope that our elementary presentation serves as good starting point for further research.
L61: ## 2 Notations
L62: Let $\mathbb{N}=\left\{0,1,2,\ldots\right\}$ be the set of non-negative integers. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we set $[n]=\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}$. For $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ we define the closed interval $[a,b]=\left\{a,a+1,a+2,\ldots,b-1,b\right\}$, and the open interval $(a,b)=\left\{a+1,a+2,\ldots,b-1\right\}$, with the half open $(a,b],[a,b)$ intervals defined similarly. We denote the symmetric group by $S_{n}:=\{\sigma:[n]\to[n]:\sigma\text{ is a bijection}\}$.
L63: Its multiplication is composition: $(ab)(i)=a(b(i))$ for all $a,b\in S_{n}$ and $i\in[n]$. We denote the identity in $S_{n}$ by $\varepsilon$. We will use $\operatorname{cyc}_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}}$ to describe a cycle in $S_{n}$, and in particular a transposition will be denoted $t_{i,j}$. We define the one-line notation of a permutation $w\in S_{n}$ to be the $n$-tuple $\operatorname{oln}\left(w\right):=\left(w\left(1\right),w\left(2\right),\dots,w\left(n\right)\right)$.
L64: When it is not ambiguous, we may omit the commas. For example, for $t_{1,2}\in S_{3}$ we may write $\operatorname{oln}{t_{1,2}}=\left(213\right)$. Occasionally, we will identify the permutation $w$ with its one-line notation.
L65: ## 3 Fixed Point Homing Shuffles
L66: 
L67: One way to characterize the shuffles we have described so far is that they always place the front card in its natural position, and do not disturb any cards numbered higher than the front card. We take these key properties as our definition of a homing shuffle.
L68: ###### Definition 3.1.
L69: 
L70: A homing shuffle is a map $\mathcal{F}:S_{n}\to S_{n}$ that satisfies the following conditions: For any $w\in S_{n}$, if we set $k:=w\left(1\right)$, then
L71: 
L72:   1. 1.
L73: 
L74: (a) We have $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)\left(k\right)=k$. Thus, $k$ is always a fixed point of $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)$.
L75: 
L76:   2. 2.
L77: 
L78: (b) We have $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)\left(i\right)=w\left(i\right)$ for all $i>k$.
L79: To keep notation concise, we will set $\mathcal{F}_{w}:=\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)$. Note that $\mathcal{F}^{k}_{w}$ will always mean $\mathcal{F}^{k}\left(w\right)$, never $\left(\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)\right)^{k}$.
L80: We may informally describe a homing shuffle as follows. Consider a deck of cards numbered $1,2,\dots,n$. If the top card is numbered $k$, take the first $k$ cards from the top of the deck. From this pile take the $k$-card and return it to the top of the deck. For the remaining cards return them to the top of the deck in any order. Specifying the order in which you return the remaining cards to the top of the deck yields different shuffles.
L81: For example, placing the remaining cards back in reverse order yields the Topswops game, while simply placing them back in their original order yields McKinley’s.
L82: We now consider some notable examples. In what follows, let us use the notation $w\overset{\mathcal{F}}{\mapsto}w^{\prime}$ as shorthand for $w^{\prime}=\mathcal{F}(w)$. Our first example is in some sense the simplest homing shuffle.
L83: ###### Example 3.2 (Transposition Shuffle).
L84: 
L85: Consider the map
L86: 
L87:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{T}:S_{n}$  | $\displaystyle\to S_{n},$  |
L88:  | $\displaystyle w$  | $\displaystyle\mapsto w\cdot t_{1,k},\qquad\text{ where }k=w\left(1\right).$  |
L89: 
L90: For example, if $w\in S_{5}$ with $\operatorname{oln}\left(w\right)=\left(23415\right)$, then (underlining the cards to be swapped in the next iteration) we see that
L91:  | $\displaystyle\left(\underline{2}\underline{3}415\right)$  | $\displaystyle\overset{\mathcal{T}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{3}2\underline{4}15\right)\overset{\mathcal{T}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{4}23\underline{1}5\right)\overset{\mathcal{T}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{1}2345\right).$  |
L92: 
L93: To see that $\mathcal{T}$ is indeed a homing shuffle, we note that condition (a) of Definition cite32†3.1 is satisfied since
L94:  | $$\mathcal{T}_{w}\left(k\right)=\left(w\cdot t_{1,k}\right)\left(k\right)=w\left(t_{1,k}\left(k\right)\right)=w\left(1\right)=k.$$  |
L95: 
L96: For all $i\not\in\left\{1,k\right\}$, we have $t_{1,k}\left(i\right)=i$ and therefore
L97: 
L98:  | $$\mathcal{T}_{w}\left(i\right)=\left(w\cdot t_{1,k}\right)\left(i\right)=w\left(t_{1,k}\left(i\right)\right)=w\left(i\right).$$  |
L99: So, in particular, if $i>k$ then $\mathcal{T}_{w}\left(i\right)=w\left(i\right)$, and condition (b) of Definition cite32†3.1 is satisfied. $\mathcal{T}$ may be described informally as the shuffle that swaps the the front card $k$ with the card currently in position $k$ of the deck.
L100: ###### Example 3.3 (McKinley’s Shuffle).
L101: 
L102: This shuffle was first studied by Gweneth McKinley in [cite28†10 ]. It is defined as the map
L103: 
L104:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}:S_{n}$  | $\displaystyle\to S_{n},$  |
L105:  | $\displaystyle w$  | $\displaystyle\mapsto w\operatorname{cyc}_{1,2,\dots,k},\qquad\text{where }k=w\left(1\right).$  |
L106: For example, considering again our permutation $w\in S_{5}$ with $\operatorname{oln}{w}=\left(23415\right)$, and underlining the portion of the one line notation to be shifted back next iteration, we see that
L107:  | $\displaystyle\left(2\underline{3}415\right)$  | $\displaystyle\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(3\underline{24}15\right)\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(2\underline{4}315\right)\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(4\underline{231}5\right)\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(2\underline{3}145\right)$  |
L108:  |  | $\displaystyle\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(3\underline{21}45\right)\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(2\underline{1}345\right)\overset{\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}}{\mapsto}\left(12345\right).$  |
L109: To see that $\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}$ is a homing shuffle, we note that
L110: 
L111:  | $$\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}\left(w\right)\left(k\right)=w\left(\operatorname{cyc}_{1,2,\dots,k}\left(k\right)\right)=w\left(1\right)=k.$$  |
L112: 
L113: And for $i>k$ we have $\operatorname{cyc}_{1,2,\dots,k}\left(i\right)=i$ so that
L114: 
L115:  | $$\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}\left(w\right)\left(i\right)=w\left(\operatorname{cyc}_{1,2,\dots,k}\left(i\right)\right)=w\left(i\right).$$  |
L116: As we stated above, $\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}$ can be described as the shuffle you get by simply placing the remaining cards (after placing the front card $k$) back on top of the deck without disturbing their original order.
L117: 
L118: For the next example we’ll introduce the reflections in $S_{n}$.
L119: ###### Definition 3.4.
L120: 
L121: If $m\in[n]$ then we define the permutation $r_{m}\in S_{n}$ by setting
L122: 
L123:  | $$r_{m}\left(i\right)=\begin{cases}m-i+1,&\text{ if }i\leq m\\
L124: i,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}$$  |
L125: 
L126: In other words, $r_{m}$ sends $1,2,\ldots,m$ to $m,m-1,\ldots,1$ and leaves the remaining elements of $[n]$ unchanged.
L127: ###### Example 3.5 (Topswops).
L128: 
L129: The topswops game was introduced by John Conway [cite20†4 , Chapter Six] (see also [cite33†3 , Aufgabe 1] and [cite21†9 , §7.2.1.2, Exercise 107]). It can be described by the following map:
L130: 
L131:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}:S_{n}$  | $\displaystyle\to S_{n},$  |
L132:  | $\displaystyle w$  | $\displaystyle\mapsto wr_{k},\qquad\text{where }k=w\left(1\right).$  |
L133: 
L134: For example, if $\operatorname{oln}{w}=\left(23415\right)$, underlining the prefix to be reversed we have
L135:  | $\displaystyle\left(\underline{23}415\right)$  | $\displaystyle\overset{\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{324}15\right)\overset{\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{4231}5\right)\overset{\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}}{\mapsto}\left(\underline{1}3245\right).$  |
L136: 
L137: Now $\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}$ is indeed a homing shuffle since
L138: 
L139:  | $$\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}\left(w\right)\left(k\right)=wr_{k}\left(k\right)=w\left(1\right)=k$$  |
L140: and $r_{k}$ fixes all $i>k$, so that $\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}\left(w\right)\left(i\right)=wr_{k}\left(i\right)=w\left(i\right)$ for all $i>k$. Described informally, $\mathcal{T}_{\text{swops}}$ is the shuffle you get by picking up the first $k$ cards and placing them back on the top of the deck in reverse order.
L141: Before we turn to an analysis of homing shuffles more generally, we first establish some simple but useful identities concerning how homing shuffles must change the deck from one iteration to the next.
L142: ###### Proposition 3.6.
L143: 
L144: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a homing shuffle, $w\in S_{n}$, and $k:=w\left(1\right)$. Then
L145: 
L146:   1. 1.
L147: 
L148: (a) We have $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i,j]\right)=w\left([i,j]\right)$ for any $k<i\leq j\leq n$.
L149: 
L150:   2. 2.
L151: 
L152: (b) We have $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i]\right)=w\left([i]\right)$ for any $i\geq k$.
L153: 
L154:   3. 3.
L155: 
L156: (c) We have $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([k-1]\right)=w\left([k]\right)\setminus\left\{k\right\}$.
L157: ###### Proof.
L158: 
L159: (a) By part (b) of Definition cite32†3.1 ,
L160: 
L161:  | $$\mathcal{F}_{w}\left(i\right)=w\left(i\right)\text{ for }i>k.$$  |
L162: 
L163: This implies $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i,j]\right)=w\left([i,j]\right)$ for $k<i\leq j\leq n$, and (a) is proved.
L164: 
L165: (b) Let $i\geq k$. Then, $k<i+1\leq n\leq n$. Thus, applying (a) to $i+1$ and $n$ instead of $i$ and $j$, we find $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i+1,n]\right)=w\left([i+1,n]\right)$. But both $\mathcal{F}_{w}$ and $w$ are permutations, and thus respect complementation:
L166:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([n]\setminus[i+1,n]\right)$  | $\displaystyle=[n]\setminus\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i+1,n]\right)\qquad\text{ and }$  |
L167:  | $\displaystyle w\left([n]\setminus[i+1,n]\right)$  | $\displaystyle=[n]\setminus w\left([i+1,n]\right).$  |
L168: The right hand sides here are equal, since $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i+1,n]\right)=w\left([i+1,n]\right)$. Thus the left hand sides are equal, i.e., we have $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([n]\setminus[i+1,n]\right)=w\left([n]\setminus[i+1,n]\right)$. But this is just saying $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([i]\right)=w\left([i]\right)$. This proves part (b).
L169: 
L170: (c) We have
L171:  | $\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([k-1]\right)$  | $\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([k]\setminus\left\{k\right\}\right)=\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([k]\right)\setminus\left\{\mathcal{F}_{w}\left(k\right)\right\}=w\left([k]\right)\setminus\left\{k\right\},$  |

L173: where the last step used the facts that $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left([k]\right)=w\left([k]\right)$ (a particular case of part (b)) and $\mathcal{F}_{w}\left(k\right)=k$ (a consequence of Definition cite32†3.1 (a)). Thus part (c). ∎
L174: ## 4 Termination Numbers
L175: The most well studied question regarding the Topswops game is concerning the longest sequence of moves. Gardner, in [cite20†4 ], asks for the “arrangement of the numbers [that] provides the longest game of topswops”. This question has been open since at least 1988 with only upper and lower bounds being known [cite20†4 , cite21†9 , cite22†11 ]. McKinley, however, determines the exact number $(2^{n-1}-1)$ for $\mathcal{M}_{\text{ck}}$ in [cite28†10 ].
L176: Here, we are interested in what we can say with regards to all homing shuffles. In this section we will show that all homing shuffles terminate in a finite number of iterations.
L177: We first note a technical point highlighted in the introduction: the game itself may continue for ever but the state no longer changes. Indeed, any further moves simply pick up the $1$-card and place it back on top of the deck. Thus, when we speak of termination, we really mean that the state is no longer changing after some iteration. This said, we begin our discussion with a simple observation.
L178: Given a homing shuffle $\mathcal{F}$ and a permutation $w\in S_{n}$, we have $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)=w$ if and only if $w\left(1\right)=1$. Indeed, if we set $k=w\left(1\right)$ as in Definition cite32†3.1 , then $k=1$ implies $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)=w$ by Definition cite32†3.1 , whereas conversely, $\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)=w$ implies $w\left(1\right)=k=\mathcal{F}\left(w\right)\left(k\right)=w\left(k\right)$ and thus $1=k$ by unapplying $w$. This leads to the following definition of termination.
L179: ###### Definition 4.1 (Termination Numbers).
L180: 
L181:   1. 1.
L182: 
L183: (a) Say that a homing shuffle $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $m$ iterations on a given permutation $w\in S_{n}$ if $\mathcal{F}^{m}_{w}\left(1\right)=1$ (or, equivalently, $\mathcal{F}^{m+1}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)$).
L184: 
L185:   2. 2.
L186: (b) The termination number of $\mathcal{F}$, denoted $\operatorname{tn}\mathcal{F}$, is the smallest $m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $m$ iterations on every $w\in S_{n}$. In other words,
L187: 
L188:  | $$\operatorname{tn}\mathcal{F}:=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb{N}\;|\;\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)\left(1\right)=1\text{ for all }w\in S_{n}\right\}.$$  |
L189: 
L190: The existence of such an $m$ is not obvious, but follows from Theorem cite30†4.7 below.
L191: ###### Proposition 4.2 (Termination is forever).
L192: 
L193: Fix a $w\in S_{n}$. Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ be such that $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $m$ iterations on $w$. Then, $\mathcal{F}^{q}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)$ for all $q\geq m$. Thus, $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $q$ iterations on $w$ for all $q\geq m$.
L194: ###### Proof.
L195: Since $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $m$ iterations on $w$, we have $\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m+1}\left(w\right)$. Applying $\mathcal{F}$ to this equality, we obtain $\mathcal{F}^{m+1}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m+2}\left(w\right)$. Applying $\mathcal{F}$ once again, we obtain $\mathcal{F}^{m+2}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m+3}\left(w\right)$.
L196: Proceeding like this indefinitely, we arrive at the chain of equalities $\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m+1}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m+2}\left(w\right)=\cdots$. In other words, $\mathcal{F}^{q}\left(w\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)$ for all $q\geq m$. This entails $\mathcal{F}^{q}\left(w\right)\left(1\right)=\mathcal{F}^{m}\left(w\right)\left(1\right)=1$ for all $q\geq m$, so that $\mathcal{F}$ terminates after $q$ iterations on $w$. ∎
L197: To illustrate let us determine the termination number of the simplest shuffle $\mathcal{T}$.
L198: ###### Theorem 4.3.
L199: 
L200: The transposition shuffle $\mathcal{T}$ terminates after $n-1$ iterations on each $w\in S_{n}$. We have
L201: 
L202:  | $$\operatorname{tn}\mathcal{T}=n-1.$$  |
L203: ###### Proof.
L204: 
L205: Let $w\in S_{n}$. Write the disjoint cycle decomposition of $w$ as follows:
L206: 
L207:  | $$w=\operatorname{cyc}_{i_{1,1},i_{1,2},\dots,i_{1,k_{1}}}\cdots\operatorname{cyc}_{i_{m,1},i_{m,2},\dots,i_{m,k_{m}}}\cdot\operatorname{cyc}_{1,w\left(1\right),w^{2}\left(1\right),\dots,w^{k}\left(1\right)},$$  |

Brief accounts of my own work on this model have appeared in conference proceedings earlier[cite27†5 , cite28†6 ].
L52: The sandpile model was proposed as a paradigm of self-organized criticality (SOC). It is certainly the simplest, and best understood, theorist’s model of SOC: it is a non-equilibrium system, driven at a slow steady rate, with local threshold relaxation rules, which in the steady state shows relaxation events in bursts of a wide range of sizes, and long-range spatio-temporal correlations, obtained without fine-tuning of any control parameters.
L53: The Abelian sandpile model (ASM) is the name given to a particular subclass of the sandpile models that have a nice mathematical structure (an abelian group). The group structure allows analytical calculation of many of the properties of the model. The mathematical tractability of the model is certainly its main attraction.
L54: In addition, the model turns out to be related to several other models in statistical mechanics: the Potts model, the voter model, directed percolation, Takayasu aggregation model etc..
L55: A different reason for the continued interest of physicists in the model is its intractability: in spite of its apparent simplicity, the original 2-dimensional BTW model has defied an analytical calculation of all critical exponents so far.
L56: The fact that the steady state for the ASM is well characterized, and allows exact calculation of averages of many physical quantities of interest ( and with only moderate effort), and that several critical exponents are known exactly, suggests that the model is ‘soluble’, and other exponents can also be determined analytically (if only we could figure out how!).

L59: The ASM is defined as follows [cite29†7 ]: we consider a lattice of $N$ sites labelled by integers $i=1$ to $N$. At each site $i$, we define a nonnegative integer height variable $z_{i}$ called the height of the sandpile, and a threshold value $z_{ic}$. If $z_{i}<z_{ic}$, for all $i$, the pile is said to be stable. The time-evolution of the sandpile is defined by the following two rules:

L61: 2. Toppling: If for any site $z_{i}\geq z_{ic}$, then that site is said to be unstable, it topples, and loses some sandgrains to other sites. This sandgrain transfer is defined in terms of an $N\times N$ integer matrix $\Delta$. On toppling at site $i$ , the configuration is updated according to the rule:

In this stationary state, relaxation after the addition of another grain typically involves a sequence of topplings. This is called an avalanche. The size of avalanche is a random variable. L305: ## 7 Concluding Remarks
L306: The sandpile is, of course, a non-equilibrium system driven by the slow addition of grains. One often finds in literature the statement that non-equilibrium systems are qualitatively different from equilibrium ones, because one cannot write a ‘well-behaved’ hamiltonian with short-ranged interactions that will show the often long-ranged correlations observed in the non-equilibrium steady states(NESS’s).
L307: But for the ASM, the NESS is characterized by a Boltzmann measure corresponding to a rather well-known equilibrium statistical mechanics model( the spanning trees or the q=0 Potts model). For the directed ASM’s, the even simpler hamiltonian H=0 is adequate.
L308: I think that the conventional wisdom is not really wrong here, because the transformation of variables needed to go from the height variables of the ASM to the spanning tree is quite complicated, and nonlocal. It preserves the probabilities of different configurations in the steady state, but the simple local rules of toppling in the ASM become complicated (and ill-understood) nonlocal evolution rules in the spanning tree description.
L309: A description directly in terms of Potts model spins is not possible because of the the formal nature of the $q\rightarrow 0$ limit.
L310: Another oft-discussed question is related to the fact that in the ASM, the time-scale of sand addition is assumed to be much longer than the time-scale of individual topplings. In fact, the existence of two very widely seperated time-scales has been argued to be one of the defining characteristics of self-organized critical systems [cite87†60 ]. But, as we have seen, the directed ASM in d-dimensions is equivalent to the Takayasu aggregation model.
L311: In the latter model, also driven, there seems to be no seperation of time-scales: aggregation and diffusion both occur at comparable rates! In addition, the distribution of avalanche-sizes in the ASM simply translates to the distribution of masses in the steady state of the second model.
L312: If we accept the existence of two time-scales as one of the defining characteristics of SOC, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable situation that the prototypical model of self-organized criticality is ‘equivalent’ to a model that does not show self-organized criticality. In this case, we cannot even resort to the argument about change of variables being complicated, as the avalanche distribution of ASM simply corresponds to the mass distribution in the Takayasu model.
L313: We conclude that the existence of two widely seperated timescales should not be considered as a necessary condition for self-organized criticality. A long-time scale can be defined by the typical seperation between suitably defined rare ‘burst’ events in the system. In the Takayasu model, these burst events are formation of large mass clusters.
L314: Before concluding, let me make a small list of questions which are not quite well understood yet.
L315: 
L316: Can one obtain the results for spanning trees, without using the heavy machinery of conformal field theory? In particular, the result that tortuisity exponent of paths on spanning trees in two dimensions is 5/4 should have a direct ’combinatorial’ derivation.
L317: 
L318: What are the exponents of the undirected ASM in two dimensions?
L319: Is it true that fractal dimension of avalanche clusters is same as space dimension for all $d\leq 4$?
L320: 
L321: Is there a systematic way to exactly compute the probabilities of avalanches of sizes $1,2\ldots$ in the undirected ASM?
L322: 
L323: What are the time-dependent correlations in avalanche sizes?

In ${\cal R}$, we can define an inverse operator $a_{i}^{-1}$ for each $i$.

Since the time evolution operator is a linear combination of different $a_{i}$’s, that is also completely diagonalized.
L129: The simplest of the sandpile models is when particle transfer occurs preferentially in one direction ( say provided by gravity). If there is no transfer in the reverse direction, the matrix $\Delta$ becomes upper triangular. Then $Det\Delta=~\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{ii}$. Thus all stable configurations are recurrent (there are no forbidden subconfigurations).
L249: We may also consider sandpile models with periodic toppling rules. Both the threshold and the transfer rules may vary from one toppling to next in a deterministic manner independently at each processor. For example, consider a sandpile model on a square lattice with toppling rules as follows: stable heights of the pile are 0 and 1. If height is greater than 1, two particles are transferred to nearest neighbors.

L289: With probability $p$, the height at the unstable site decreases by $2$, and one particle is transferred to each downward neighbor. with probability $(1-p)$, no transfer takes place. In either case, the site becomes stable for the next time step. At any time, only sites where at least one particle was added at the last step can become unstable [cite84†57 ].
